en: Regarding alms-food, the eightfold *piṇḍaniryukti* consists of: origin (*uggama*), procurement (*uppāyaṇa*), inspection (*esaṇā*), mixing (*jōyaṇā*), quantity (*pamāṇa*), charcoal (*iṅgāla*), smoke (*dhūma*), and cause (*kāraṇa*). — PiṇḍNi.1
*Piṇḍa*, *nikāya*, *samūha*, *sampiṇḍana*, *piṇḍanā*, *samavāya*, *samusaraṇa*, *nicaya*, *upacaya*, *caya*, *yugma*, and *rāśi* [are synonyms]. —
PiṇḍNi.2
The exposition of the *piṇḍa* (alms-food) should be performed fourfold or sixfold;
having performed the exposition, its detailed explanation (*prarūpaṇā*) must be carried out.
— PiṇḍNi.3 —
In a *kula* there is the occurrence of one-fourth [of the group], while in a *chaṅga* there is necessarily the occurrence of four; therefore, one should deposit the *chaṅga*. (Piṇḍaniyukti 4)
The enumeration of the types of alms (piṇḍa) is indeed sixfold: by name, by substance, by field, by time, and by state. This is the classification of alms. (Piṇḍaniyukti 5)
That which is metaphorical, that which is based on convention, or that which is produced by both—these they call the "name-aggregate" (*nāmapinda*).
Next, I shall explain the "representation-aggregate" (*ṭhavaṇāpinda*).
(PiṇḍNi 6)
That which is produced from qualities is figurative (goṇṇa), and that very same [term] is called "according to the actual meaning" (jahattha) by the masters;
furthermore, that [is exemplified as] Khavaṇa, Jalaṇa, Tavaṇa, Pavaṇa, and Paīva. (PiṇḍNi. 7)

Where there is a designation of "alms" (*piṇḍa*) even by way of an antonym for a collection of many substances, that is a "conventional alms" (*samayakṛta-piṇḍa*), as in the Sūtra on the Acceptance of Alms (*Piṇḍapāta*). (PiṇḍNi.
But for one who has entered for the sake of alms-food and obtains a portion consisting of molasses and boiled rice, that they call "alms-food of both kinds" (tadubhayapiṇḍa). (Piṇḍaniyukti 9)
Indeed, there is also another kind of worldly [scripture] that exceeds both [the Vedas and the Āgamas],
namely that which is composed according to one's own whim, such as those by Siṃha, Devadatta,
and others. (Piṇḍaniryukti 10)
A figurative name that is not literal, or another name suggested by a hint—just as the name "Piṇḍa" is given to a certain person—is what is called a *sūiya* (hinted) name.
(PiṇḍNi. 11)
Even when their intentions are identical, people do not adopt what is established by [sectarian] tradition;
rather, those who have attained equanimity (sāmāyika) practice that which is established by common worldly consensus.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 12)
Whether it be in an eye, a coin, wood, a clay model, or a painting—
whether representing reality or unreality— know this to be *thāvanā-piṇḍa* (representational alms).
(Piṇḍanijjutti 13)
In the case of an unreal object, there is the establishment of the three [types of images]; however, in the case of a real object, it occurs among mental states.
When the object is unreal, it is like a wooden image or a plaster image; when it is real, it is like a reflection in water.
(Piṇḍanijjutti 14)
Substance-food (dravyapiṇḍa) is threefold: with living beings (sacitta), mixed (mīsa), and without living beings (acitta).
Furthermore, for each of these, there are nine sub-divisions respectively. (Gāthā 16, Piṇḍaniryukti 15)
Earth, water, fire, air, and plants; as well as those with two sense-faculties, three sense-faculties, four sense-faculties, and five sense-faculties. (Piṇḍaniryukti 16)
The earth-body is threefold: with consciousness, mixed, and without consciousness.
Furthermore, that which is with consciousness is twofold: according to the ultimate sense (nischaya) and according to the conventional sense (vyavahāra). (Piṇḍaniryukti 17)
According to the definitive [classification], that which is in the very center of great earth-mountains is non-living with a slight admixture;
the rest is conventionally considered living.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 18)
On the path beneath a milk-tree, on a wooden plank, or with fuel, it is mixed;
[the time for alms] is one, two, or three *pauruṣīs*, and when there is much fuel, it is at the end of the middle watch.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 19)
Because [the womb] is produced from what has been ejected—namely, cold, heat, alkaline, salty, fire-like, pungent, sour, oily, and so forth—therefore this [body] comes to be. (PiṇḍNī.
Just as poison is neutralized by an antidote, or salt by fragrant rock-salt, so too is the apprehension of that which is insentient; this is the purpose of this and other [rules].
(Piṇḍaniryukti 21)

Standing, sitting, lying down, as well as the disposal of excrement and so forth, the sweeping of the ground, and the removal of dust, dregs, and plaster— these are the many purposes [for which one may step outside]. (Piṇḍaniyukti 22)
The water element is threefold: with consciousness (*sacitta*), mixed (*mīsa*), and without consciousness (*acitta*).
Furthermore, that which is with consciousness is twofold: according to ultimate reality (*nicchaya*) and according to conventional usage (*vavahāra*). (Piṇḍaniryukti 23)
In the very midst of the oceans of clouds, the enclosures of clouds, and the lakes of the Karaka ocean,
that which is determined to be with consciousness by the *niścaya-naya* is, according to the *vyavahāra-naya*,
not a jar. (Piṇḍaniryukti 24)
When the staff [of the sun] follows hot water and rain has fallen just once,
one should leave aside three measures of husks and take rice-water that is not too clear.
(Piṇḍaniyukti 25)
As long as the froth clinging to the edge of the vessel does not subside, and as long as the rice grains mixed with other things are still being cooked, [one should not eat]. (Piṇḍaniyukti 26)
These three, moreover, are not independent [factors], because the restriction of time is impossible;
they depend on whether dry or other types of goods, wind, and so forth are present or absent.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 27)
As long as it is not mostly pure, it is mixed; this is the rule here.
When it is mostly pure, however, it should be known as non-living (inanimate).
(Piṇḍaniryukti 28)
Cold, heat, salt, alkaline, fire, salt-earth,
sour, and oily substances— this is the purpose served by that which has its source in the womb.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 29)
Washing the hands after drinking cold water, washing robes, rinsing the mouth, and cleaning the bowl— such purposes for washing are manifold.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 30)
Unbinding [the hair],
rubbing it dry, the destruction of celibacy, placing [an object] in an improper place, the killing of wind-breaths, and the injury to living beings.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 31)

In the rainy season, there are faults in the distribution of food: [the food] becomes heavy to carry, it spoils, it becomes cold, it is difficult to digest, it causes illness, it leads to humiliation, and there is injury to the body; furthermore, there are faults regarding the washing of the feet. (Gāthā 33, Piṇḍaniryukti 32)
Even when it has not rained, they shake out their entire equipment with care;
in the absence of [other] materials, at the very least, the equipment for the alms-bowl must be shaken out.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 33)
The teachers and the sick wash their robes again and again even when they are already soiled, lest there be censure of the elders in the world; for others, it would lead to indigestion.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 34)
The equipment for the alms-bowl consists of the two types of seats (dunisijja), the three cloths (tipaṭṭa), the undergarment (potti), and the dust-remover (rayaharaṇa).
These, however, require no rest; rather, they require careful handling, shifting, and cleaning.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 35)
The arrangement for the drinking vessel consists of the bowl itself and the accessories for the drinking vessel; furthermore, there are two seats:
the inner and the outer. (Piṇḍaniyukti 36)
It should be known that there are three [types of] garments: the *santhāra* (bedding), the *uttaracōlaga* (upper robe), and the *paṭṭa* (waistband);
as well as the mouth-cloth (*muhapottiyā*), the cloth (*pottī*), the single seat (*ēganisejjā*), and the dust-remover (*rayaharaṇa*).
(PiṇḍNi 37)

But these [monks] do not wash [the bowls] during the rest period; rather, having transferred them with care according to the rule, they wash them there at the proper time, following the procedure for the six verses of the *Vidyā*.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 38)
Furthermore, as for resting:
when it is time to wash the robes, having thus obtained permission according to the command of the Vītarāga (the One Free from Passion), the monk may rest his requisites.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 39)
One should attain internal enjoyment [of the alms] not too far above;
having grouped them three by three, one should then determine [the portions]. (Piṇḍaniyukti 40)

A cloth that has been washed [is considered pure] for three days; thereafter it reaches the state of being "near" (āsanna) for another three days; and after that, it remains hanging [as impure] for one day.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 41)
Some, having lived together for a year, recognize [the disciple] there;
if the six verses do not stick, they wash him away with them. (PiṇḍNi.
Some say that there is a prohibition against accepting water that has not been strained;
however, there is no prohibition regarding impurity when it concerns the vessels of householders. In the case of rain that has fallen and remains standing, it is considered mixed with ash.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 43)
First, one should wash the feet of the guru, those who have renounced [food], the sick, the *śaikṣas*, and so forth;
then one's own, then the two [other] types of *mahākaḍa* (those who have performed great penance), and finally the others.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 44)
One should not shake or beat [the robes]; one should not wash what has already been washed, nor perform the drying;
one should examine whether they are fit for use or unfit for use, and consider the shade and the sun for their preservation.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 45)
Fire is of three kinds: with consciousness (*sacitta*), mixed (*mīsa*), and without consciousness (*acitta*).
Furthermore, that which is with consciousness is twofold: according to the ultimate standpoint (*nicchaya*) and according to the conventional standpoint (*vavahāra*). (Piṇḍaniryukti 46)
In the midst of many bricks and stones, it is certainly "lightning-like";
among charcoal and the like, it is "otherwise" (dark); and among glowing embers and the like, it is "mixed.
(Piṇḍaniyukti 47)
Rice gruel, condiments, drinks, water for rinsing the mouth, warm water, and boiled rice— these,
along with clods of earth, pebbles, charcoal, needles, long pepper, and so forth,
constitute objects of utility. (Piṇḍaniryukti 48)
The air-element is threefold: with consciousness (*sacitta*), mixed (*miśra*), and without consciousness (*acitta*).

Furthermore, that which is with consciousness is twofold: from the perspective of ultimate reality (*niścaya*) and from the perspective of conventional practice (*vyavahāra*). (Gāthā 50, Piṇḍaniryukti 49)
In a cloudy day with thick mist and in a very stormy day,
both the conventional (vyavahāra) and the absolute (niścaya) [standpoints] agree that [the food] has been stepped over and is therefore insentient (acitta).
(Piṇḍaniryukti 50)
When stepped upon, trodden down, smelled, followed by the body,
or subjected to pressure and so forth, the insentient air-element is described as such by those who destroy the eight types of karma.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 51)
Having gone one hundred cubits, it is insentient; in the second [hundred], it is mixed; but in the third, the bladder is sentient.
Furthermore, regarding the periods of the day, [the following applies]. (Piṇḍaniyukti 52)
The time for the removal [of moisture] is also of three kinds: exclusively moist, moderate, and low; and the dry [time] is likewise threefold: low, moderate, and high. (Piṇḍaniryukti 53)
In the first stage, the bladder is entirely moist;
in the second, it is insentient; in the third, it is mixed; and in the third [stage], the bladder becomes sentient.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 54)
In the middle watch, wind is insentient; in the second watch, it is mixed; in the third and fourth watches, it is sentient; and when it has entered the middle of the body, it is given as food.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 55)
In the first [day] one abandons non-living things; in the second, mixed things; in the fourth, living things;
and in the fifth, even coarse food is abandoned. Thus, there is an increase in what is given.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 56)
If there should be a need for a vessel made of leather or one made of wood, or if a sage should have an illness, he may use it;
however, he should avoid those that are mixed with living beings.
(PiṇḍNi 57)
Forest vegetation is threefold: with consciousness (*sacitta*), mixed (*miśra*), and without consciousness (*acitta*).
Furthermore, that which is with consciousness is twofold: according to ultimate reality (*niścaya*) and according to conventional practice (*vyavahāra*). (Piṇḍaniryukti 58)
According to the ultimate standpoint (*niścayanaya*), everything that possesses consciousness is infinite;
according to the conventional standpoint (*vyavahāranaya*), the rest is mixed, such as the flour-cake and so forth.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 59)
When the stalks of flowers, leaves, clusters of fruit, and likewise of greenery have withered, one should know that they are abandoned by life. (Piṇḍaniryukti 60)
The bedding, the staff, the woolen cloth, the apron, the seats, the wooden planks, and the medicinal herbs and remedies— these serve many purposes in this way. (Piṇḍaniryukti 61)
Two, three, four, or five sense-faculties (indriya) are present;
wherever they converge in their respective places, that is "alms-food" (piṇḍa), and by means of it, this purpose is accomplished. (PiṇḍNi.
The consumption of two-sensed beings refers to things such as conchs and moon-crystals;
for three-sensed beings, it refers to creatures like earthworms (*uddēhikā*) or whatever a physician might prescribe.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 63)

In the case of food involving five sense organs, there is indeed avoidance of fish and avoidance of [food] observed by others; however, those who do not practice restraint regarding the alms-food of the five senses are hell-beings. (Piṇḍaniryukti 64)
The five-sensed animals provide the enjoyment [of their products] as hides, bones, teeth, hair, horns, wool, dung, cow-urine, milk, curds, and so forth. (Piṇḍaniryukti 65)

In the case of animate [food], there is the initiation of one's own mind, instruction on the path, and the giving of alms; in the case of bone [as food], there is the head-bone, the mixed bone, the protected bone, and the inquiry regarding the road. (Gāthā 67, Piṇḍaniryukti 66)

When a mendicant is about to set out on a journey or when his time of death has arrived, he may inquire of some deity regarding the auspiciousness or inauspiciousness of the path; this is the divine application (*divya-upayoga*).
(Piṇḍaniryukti 67)
Now, the mixed alms-food (*mīsa-ōya-piṇḍa*) of these same nine types of alms-food should be understood as arising from combinations of two and so forth, up to the final [combination]. (PiṇḍNi.
Sour gruel, milk-ferment, dhal-flour, medicinal oils, soups with fruits,
salted grains, molasses, and rice-porridge— these various types of alms-food arise from combinations [of ingredients].
(Piṇḍaniryukti 69)
The three pradeśasamayas (space-points per moment) are the durations of the states of the substance;
that is the exposition of the four and five piṇḍas wherever and whenever their description occurs.
(PiṇḍNi 70)

If a composite whole is appropriate in the case of liberated substances due to their mutual interpenetration, then it is also appropriate in the case of those liberated from matter, because of the abundance of atoms. (PiṇḍNi.
Just as a three-partite aggregate (skandha) is equally immersed in all three parts and is connected as an indivisible whole, how could its substratum not be likewise? (PiṇḍNi.

Alternatively, it is appropriate that the alms-food (piṇḍa) belongs necessarily to all four [divisions] through the distribution of their functions; however, in two of them, the alms-food is either described or actually prepared. (PiṇḍNi.
The substance-aggregate (bhāvapiṇḍa), moreover, is of two kinds: commendable and non-commendable. I shall explain the exposition of each of these two separately. (PiṇḍNi 74)
The single-fold and ten-fold [types of conduct] are indeed commendable as well as non-commendable;
restraint, knowledge-conduct, and the triad beginning with knowledge are each threefold. (Piṇḍaniryukti 75)

One should understand knowledge, vision, austerity, and self-restraint; the five vows, the six [rules], the rules for seeking alms-food, the rules for seeking water, and the formal procedures for receiving gifts regarding food.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 76)

The nine principles of the teaching, the nine protections of celibacy, and likewise the duty of the ascetic— this is declared as the "alms-food" (piṇḍa) by those who destroy the eight types of karma. (PiṇḍNi 77)
Blame, lack of self-restraint, ignorance, lack of renunciation, and false belief;
anger and the other influxes, the physical activities, lack of protection, and violence—these are the causes of karma.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 78)
That by which karma is bound is entirely unwholesome;
however, that by which one is liberated is to be understood as exclusively wholesome.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 79)
Whatever and however many modifications there are of right vision, knowledge, and conduct, each of those constitutes a modification; this is the summary of the enumeration of modifications. (PiṇḍNī.

By whatever state of being one accumulates for oneself a thick mass of karma, that becomes the "state-mass" (*bhāvapiṇḍa*); it is called *piṇḍa* because it is accumulated (*piṇḍayati*) by means of accumulation (*piṇḍana*). — Piṇḍaniyukti 81.

In this context, the substance is insentient and the state is commendable through knowledge; the practice is undertaken for the purpose of transforming the intellect so that it conforms to the meaning of what has been proclaimed.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 82)
One makes a proper acceptance of food, clothing, and bedding, as well as of recommended alms;
regarding food, it is pure through eight points. (Gāthā 84, Piṇḍaniryukti 83)
Nirvana is indeed the goal, and the triad beginning with knowledge (jñāna) is its cause;
furthermore, food becomes the cause of those causes of Nirvana. (Piṇḍaniryukti 84)
Just as the threads are the cause of a cloth, and for those [threads] there are various colors, so too is food the cause for this triplefold path leading to liberation. (Piṇḍaniryukti 85)
Just as a cause that is fully supported brings about its effect necessarily and without deficiency, so too do knowledge and the other [faculties] when they are unimpaired. (Piṇḍaniryukti 86)
Thus, the summarized meaning of the *piṇḍa* has been fully explained by me; now I shall speak of *eṣaṇā* for the sake of clarity, explicitness, and manifestation. (PiṇḍNi.
Eṣaṇā, gaveṣaṇā, mārgaṇā, and uggovaṇā (udgrahaṇā) should be understood; these are indeed synonyms for eṣaṇā. (PiṇḍNi.
The search for food (eṣaṇā) should be understood as being twofold: pertaining to substances and pertaining to states of being.
Each of these two types, whether regarding substances or states of being, should be understood as being threefold.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 89)
One seeks birth;
another seeks the food of his son; another seeks a lost enemy; and another seeks death by means of poison.
(Piṇḍanijjutti 90)
In this very same way, regarding the remaining cases— quadrupeds, bipeds, inanimate,
and mixed— one should apply that specific mode of seeking (eṣaṇā) which is appropriate in each respective instance.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 91)

The search for alms (bhāveṣaṇā) is threefold; it should be understood as the search for seeking (gaveṣaṇā), the search for grasping (grahaṇeṣaṇā), and the search for consumption (gāseṣaṇā), taught in succession by those free from passion.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 92)
There is no grasping of what has not been sought, nor is there consumption of what has not been grasped;
this is the sequence for the threefold scrutiny (*eṣaṇā-trika*) that must be understood. (Piṇḍaniryukti 93)
Investigation should be understood as being fourfold: regarding name (*nāman*), representation (*sthāpanā*), substance (*dravya*), and state (*bhāva*).
Regarding substance, one should investigate the origin (*udgama*) and procurement (*utpādanā*); regarding state, one should investigate the deer-like [impurity] (*kuraṅga-gatā*).
(Piṇḍaniryukti 94)
The entry of Jiyasattu’s queen into the assembly hall, her sitting upon a golden seat,
the inquiry regarding her pregnancy-longing (dōhalaka), the narration [of the dream], and the command given to the men.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 95)
The making of a golden vessel as a gift, and the analogies for the auspicious and inauspicious arrival of deer beneath golden trees.
(Piṇḍanijjutti 96)
This is another marvel of deer:
that even when the wind blows from the north, it formerly used to blow in dense clusters, yet now it does not. (Piṇḍaniyukti 97)
In the summer, there is the seizing of elephants, the filling of lakes with water-wheels,
the harvesting of reeds by the intense heat, and the arrival of herds of wild elephants.
(Piṇḍaniyukti 98)
This is the nature of herds of elephants:
when they grow reeds, at other times they discharge streams, yet these are not so abundant with water. (Piṇḍaniyukti 99)
*Uggama*, *uggovaṇa*, and *maggaṇā* are synonyms for these [terms].
Apprehension (*uggaha*) occurs in four ways: as name (*nāma*), representation (*ṭhavaṇā*), substance (*davva*), and mode (*bhāva*).
(Gāthā 101, Piṇḍaniryukti 100)
Regarding substance, there are sweets and the like;
regarding disposition, the threefold origination is to be understood as pertaining to vision, knowledge, and conduct. Here, however, the focus is on the origination of conduct.
(PiṇḍNi. 101)
Regarding the origin of substances for those who desire the excellence of yoga and who are free from deceit:
furthermore, that origin of substances must be understood as to what it is, when it occurs, and how it arises.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 102)
In the Vāsahara, Anujatta, Atthāṇī, and Jogga regions, as well as during the time for play, balls were fashioned from clay jars and bowls for the one who loved sweetmeats (Laḍḍukapiya). (PiṇḍNi.
[The diseases] arise from two types of impurities (*mala*): those originating from food and those originating from thought.
Those originating from food arise from indigestion, wind (*māruta*), or natural constitution; those originating from thought arise from anxiety regarding the acquisition of food.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 104)
For him, through such an ascent of detachment (*vairāgya*), there arose simultaneously the emergence of right faith, knowledge, and conduct, or else the emergence of omniscience (*kevalajñāna*).
(PiṇḍNī. 105)
Conduct arises from right vision and knowledge; their purity comes through that conduct.
Through conduct, there is purity from karma, which results from purity in the procurement of alms (udgama), and thereby purity of conduct is achieved.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 106)

[Food] produced for a specific purpose (āhākamma), that which is designated for a specific person (uddesiya), that which is impure through ritual preparation (pūīkamma), that which is mixed (mīsajāya), stored food (ṭhavaṇā), food received as a gift (pāhuḍiyā), food obtained by pressure (pāōara), bought food (kīya), and borrowed food (pāmicca).
— Piṇḍaniryukti 107.
[Food] that has been carried around, brought [from afar], split open, brought on a garland,
taken by force, not permitted, and the sixteenth, which is stored up.
(Piṇḍaniyukti 108)
*Āhākammiya* and *nāma* are synonyms. To whom [does it apply], or what [is it]?
Regarding the opposing side (*parapakkha*) and one's own side (*sapakkha*), there are four types: taking [food] and so forth, as well as commands (*āṇā*).
(Piṇḍaniyukti 109)

Alms-food, day-to-day life, karma, self-karma, self-action, as well as practicing [forbidden acts], consenting [to them], living together [with transgressors], and approval [of such acts]. (Piṇḍaniryukti 110)
The shoulders and heart of those who bear the burden of the bow, as well as the responsibilities of family and state, are indeed exhausted at the end of the bowstring. (PiṇḍNi.
That which is performed for the sake of someone—having directed the mind toward them—for the purpose of massaging their noble bodies or fanning them, they call that *āhākamma*. (PiṇḍNi.
By the term "taking hold of the *ūrāla* (gross body)," one should understand the killing of animals or humans, excluding those that are subtle (*sūkṣma*).
Furthermore, know that "uprooting" refers to causing pain while avoiding actual slaughter. (Piṇḍaniyukti 113)
There are three types of soul: the bodily, the mental, and the third; or alternatively, the soul as body, as sense organ, and as vital breath.
These threefold [classifications] apply to ownership, acquisition, and the instruments.
(Piṇḍaniyukti 114)

Having concentrated the mind within, he who performs the act of taking— whether of one thing or many things— with his body, that is "acquisition through the body" (kāyēṇa tamāhakammaṃ). (Piṇḍaniryukti 115)
That substance which sinks when thrown into water and so forth, or that which goes down due to its weight or by means of a cool rope, is "substance-aided action" (*davvahēkamma*). — PiṇḍNi.

It establishes the state of the stages of restraint (*saṃyama-sthāna*), the groups (*kaṇḍaka*), and the specific levels of the leśyās; therefore, it is called *bhāvādhikarma*. (Gāthā 118, Piṇḍaniryukti 117)
In that regard, the infinite modes of conduct (*caritta-paryāya*) exist; those [modes] are numerable as places of restraint (*saṃyama-sthāna*).
These should be known as a "stratum" (*kaṇḍaka*).
(PiṇḍNi. 118)
The number of "sections" (kaṇḍaka) is indeed finite; the "sixfold place" (ṣaṭsthānaka) has been pointed out.
However, the "ladder of restraint" (saṃyamaśreṇī) should be understood as having infinite sixfold places.
(PiṇḍNī 119)

Regarding the black and other leśyās, due to the distinctions of their maximum degree of purity and duration, one who grasps even a small amount of these pure [leśyās] performs [merit]. (Piṇḍaniryukti 120)
Alas, alas! One who accepts food prepared specifically for him (āhākamma) and who lacks even a fraction of the practice of self-restraint leads himself to ruin.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 121)

One binds the duration of existence (bhavāyu) here below; one seizes karmas that face downwards through intense activity and a violent state of being; this constitutes decrease and increase [of karma]. (PiṇḍNi.

If one were to scatter [the food] after searching for it, or if it were to fall near [the vessel], or if the vessel were to break— in the same way, even in the case of a sick person, there would be the transfer of the illness and public scandal.
(Piṇḍaniyukti 624)
Public scandal, falling from one's body, blindness, fear, and being struck by a bystander;
for one who has committed such faults, there is the transfer [of the offense], as well as when the flesh is oozing and the body is broken.
(Piṇḍaniyukti 625)
Falling while wearing sandals; when they are bound [to the feet], there is suffering, impurity, and reproach;
and the same [impurity and reproach] apply to the hands, as well as falling with the feet.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 626)

In the case of taking food from one who is not a monk, there are faults pertaining to oneself, others, or both; there is agitation, the possibility of being a neuter, and public loathing and suspicion, thinking, "Surely these people are of such a nature. (Gāthā 628, Piṇḍaniryukti 627)
Furthermore, for a pregnant woman, there may be physical trauma to the fetus;
as she moves about, she might harm the child, the flesh-eating cat, or other such creatures.
(Piṇḍaniyukti 628)
While eating, if one drops water while sipping, there is public reproach;
if one grinds [the food], it becomes a source of attachment when the hand is smeared with flavors.
(Piṇḍaniyukti 629)
In a mortar, during the rubbing, grinding, pounding, splitting,
crushing, burning, winnowing, and plucking [of grain], water is given to the hands when they are smeared [with flour].
(Piṇḍaniyukti 630)
Salt water, raw grain, fruits, fish, and the like, having been placed in the hand,
[if taken] with the foot, involve immersion, contact, and the consumption of the remainder. (Piṇḍaniyukti 631)
While digging, one may scrape, rub, wash, or sprinkle something;
or, being skilled in cutting, one cuts at the sixth [layer] while it is quivering. (Piṇḍaniryukti 632)
Some, with their hands grasping the six types of living beings, carry away *kolā* and *ai-kannala* plants,
as well as *siddhatthaka* flowers placed upon their heads. (Piṇḍaniryukti 633)

Others say that among the ten faults of seeking (eṣaṇā-doṣas), there is no mention of this [the donor]; therefore, it is not called a fault. But is it not true that "seeking" (grahaṇa) is indeed included within the "seeking of the giver" (dāyakagrahaṇa)? (Piṇḍaniyukti 634)
In a place where there is attachment, the movement of the hand smeared with substances that cause attachment constitutes "seeking" (ōyattaṇa);
even when [the food] is being lifted up, those same [faults] apply. (Piṇḍaniyukti 635)

That which is common to many: therein, as in the case of what has not been assigned, there are faults such as theft, seizure, and fear, or [the accusation] from a daughter-in-law regarding [the consumption of] food.
(Piṇḍaniyukti 636)
The faults regarding food placed for one's arrival (*pāhuḍi-ṭhaviya*) are threefold: in the [three] realms of hell-beings, animals, and humans; and the dangers are likewise threefold.
Food that is righteous (*dhammiya*) and so forth may be set aside either for another person or for the sake of another’s sanctity (*parasantiya*).
(Piṇḍaniyukti 637)
Out of compassion for those who oppose him, he acts even though he knows the faults of seeking alms; the second type acts without deceit, being unaware [of those faults]. (PiṇḍNi.
When alms are being given by a child, there is no investigation;
however, when [the giver] has been instructed, or when it is very much, taking [the food] is permitted upon investigation.
(PiṇḍNi 639)
The Elder, trembling, should be supported by another person who possesses a firm body, or by one who is indistinctly intoxicated,
or by one who is not confused,
or by one who is not envious. (Piṇḍaniyukti 640)
When one's own body is afflicted by intense pain and one is trembling due to old age, a lay follower (śrāvaka) or someone else should hold him while he gives food;
or he may be held by another while giving. (Piṇḍaniryukti 641)
One who has been born into the maṇḍala [of the saṅgha], one who is not a companion, one who has put on his shoes, one who is immovable,
one bound by karma, one who is playful, and another who is established as a non-companion.
(PiṇḍNi 642)
A eunuch, one who does not practice [the rule], one who lives by the shore, one who lives by breasts, and all others [of this kind]—
if the bowl has been lifted up and there is no rain, nothing sticks to it as it stands.
(Piṇḍaniyukti 643)

One who grinds [grains] until they are flourless, or one who grinds [them] comfortably, or one who cuts [vegetables] without attachment, or one who deals with powdered conch-shell or other powders, or one who is not a washerwoman—[these are the types of women]. (Gāthā 645; Piṇḍanijjutti 644)
Nor does one touch a bone that has been discarded by one associated with the *uvvaṭṭaṇī* (the process of discarding);
furthermore, there is no subsequent action (*pacchākamma*) regarding winnowing or crushing where such [faults] do not exist. (Piṇḍaniyukti 645)
In the remaining cases, such as the taking of the body and so forth, no opposite [action] is possible;
and in the absence of an opposite, the grasping of that [object] necessarily occurs. (Piṇḍaniryukti 646)

In the case of one's own mind, another's mind, both mixed, and unmixed, there are four permutations; a prohibition applies to the first three, while in the final permutation there is an option. (Piṇḍaniyukti 647)

Just as the combinations of bodies are described below in the section on "withdrawal" (*sāharaṇa*), so too they are in the "mixing" (*ummīsa*); however, there is this specific distinction therein: *PiṇḍNi* 648.

Mixing both types of substances—those that may be accepted and those that may not—such as boiled rice and raw grain, and then giving them away by placing some in one vessel and discarding others elsewhere; [this constitutes a *sādhāraṇa* offense].
(Piṇḍaniyukti 649)
Just as four types of hemp are mixed with dry [substances] that are themselves dry, so too are there four [types of] conduct regarding what is customary and what is not customary,
whether in small or large quantities.
(Piṇḍaniyukti 650)
Non-conversion (*apariṇāma*) is also twofold: in substance (*dravya*) and in state (*bhāva*). Each of these two is further twofold.
In the case of substance, there is a sixfold [classification]; in the case of state, there are the "Sajjhilagas" (the five stages of spiritual progress).
(Piṇḍaniryukti 651)
While the living being has not departed, it is untransformed; once the living being has departed, it is transformed.
The illustration is like milk and curd: that which is untransformed and that which is transformed.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 652)
If two or more things are to be shared equally, and one is given to a single person while the rest are not,
then from the perspective of intention (*bhāva*), this is considered "unshared. (Piṇḍaniyukti 653)
Even if this [fault] has been considered by only one among them in his mind, and not by the others, that too indeed becomes unacceptable;
whether it be a novice, a householder, or a monk.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 654)

"One should accept food that has been smeared with a coating, provided it is already coated; one must avoid subsequent processing (*pacchakamma*) and attachment to flavors. When this was said, the *Cōyaga* (the challenger) says:
[PiṇḍNi. 655]

If there are faults due to subsequent actions (paścātkarma), one should simply not eat at all; O student, for one who endures [these hardships], there is no loss of austerity, restraint, and self-control.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 656)

Having spoken thus, for six months one should diminish [the meal] by one [portion] at a time; however, the practice of *āyambila* (eating only boiled rice) should be undertaken on the fourth day, provided there is no bedding and it involves little impurity. (PiṇḍNi.

Having continuously observed the *āyambila* fast for six months during the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*), if one is unable to complete it within those six months, then one may perform it minus a single day. (PiṇḍNi.
Having thus exhausted the *āyambilapāraṇa* for each individual day, one should daily undertake the *āyambila* itself until it is completed. (PiṇḍNi.

If there is no loss of yoga at present, or if it occurs in this manner, one should practice forgiveness; otherwise, by means of further forgiveness, one performs the austerity of the *āyambila* vow. (PiṇḍNi.
If even those humans of the lower regions— who eat kola-fruit, sour gruel,
and boiled rice— can attain liberation, why indeed should ascetics not attain it? (Gāthā 662,
Piṇḍaniryukti 661)
It is cold for ascetics and hot for householders; therefore, the taking of buttermilk and similar substances is permitted.
However, regarding substances such as *kaṭṭara* (sour gruel), it must be considered with discrimination.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 662)
Food, clothing, and bedding—these three are warm for householders even when it is cold; therefore, their food is digested by heat from both sides. (Piṇḍaniyukti 663)
These same three things are cold even for ascetics during the summer; therefore, fire harms them, and from that arise faults such as indigestion.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 664)
Rice gruel, rice porridge, wheat flour, parched grain, sesame balls,
peas, lentils, mung beans, black gram, and dried beans— these are dry foods.
(Piṇḍaniyukti 665)
Ubbhijja-piyyakaṅgū, takka, ollaṇa, sūva, kañji, and kaḍhiyā—these are indeed with little residue; therein, the subsequent action (pacchākamma) is to be understood. (PiṇḍNi 666)
Milk, curd, flour, hard food, oil, ghee, molasses, meat broth, and so forth—such extensive *paścātkarma* (subsequent preparation) is necessarily present there. (PiṇḍNi.

Like a drunkard with his hand stuck in a vessel, one who has remnants of food must necessarily take [the remainder] from these eight cases; however, the taking [of alms] occurs only when these conditions are absent. (PiṇḍNi.
Regarding the presence of living beings (*sacitta*), the absence of living beings (*accitta*), the mixture (*mīsaga*), and discarding (*chaḍḍaṇa*), there are four permutations (*caubhaṅga*).
In each of these four permutations, there is a prohibition; in the case of taking [the food], there are faults such as violating the command (*āṇā*) and so forth.
(Piṇḍaniyukti 669)
If one discards hot [food], one might burn oneself or suffer a bodily inflammation; if cold [rain] falls, there is the example of the drop of honey falling upon the body. (Piṇḍaniryukti 670)
The search for food (ghāseṣaṇā) should be understood as being fivefold: by name (nāma), representation (ṭhavaṇā), substance (davva), and state (bhāva).
Regarding substance, it is the catching of fish; regarding state, it is fivefold. (PiṇḍNi.
Conduct and what is appropriate— these two types of requisites should be understood as the means for accomplishing one's purpose, like fuel for the sake of cooking. (Piṇḍaniyukti 672)
When the flesh had been discarded, the fish said to the meditating crab: "Why do you meditate thus? Listen first to how you have become shameless. (Piṇḍaniyukti 673)
One who has been released from the mouth of a fishhook three times, and whose arm has been cut by a net seven times, will burn in hell for as many aeons. (Piṇḍaniyukti 674)
To seize by the throat such a being as me—one who is deceitful and strikes back at every blow—oh, what shamelessness you possess! (PiṇḍNi.

O living being! In this dense thicket of the forty-two faults of alms-gathering, you have indeed not been deceived now; act so that you may not be deceived while consuming [food] through passion and aversion. (Piṇḍaniryukti 676)
Regarding the search for food, it is considered commendable in its true nature as well as non-commendable;
the non-commendable is fivefold, while the commendable is the opposite of that. (Piṇḍaniryukti 677)

Regarding attachment (*sañjōyaṇā*), there is that of substance (*davva*) and that of state (*bhāva*). Attachment of substance is twofold: external and internal. While wandering for alms, [attachment] toward the external is that which occurs while one is actually collecting [food]. (Gāthā 679;
Piṇḍaniryukti 678)

When milk, curd, oil, or solid food is obtained, as well as molasses, ghee, cakes, or *vāluṅka* fruit, there is a threefold internal [classification]; however, regarding the mouthful (*lambaṇa*) and the face, there is a distinction.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 679)
The fault in mixing is that he who mixes food and drink with other substances for the sake of taste incurs this obstruction. (Piṇḍaniryukti 680)
Furthermore, regarding the state of attachment (*sañjōyaṇā*): having joined those substances together, one joins them with karma;
through karma there is existence (*bhava*), and from that comes suffering (*dukkha*). (PiṇḍNi.

When the alms-bowl has been received, the meal has been consumed, and the remainder has been disposed of, the remaining [sequence] for departing is observed; indeed, this is the "order according to sequence" (*yathākrama*) in that regard.
(Piṇḍaniyukti 682)

The mixing [of flavors] for the sake of taste is forbidden; however, it is permitted for the sake of one who is ill, or for one who has a desire for food, or for one who is accustomed to comfort, or for one who is not yet spiritually refined.
(Piṇḍaniyukti 683)
It is said that thirty-two mouthfuls constitute a meal that fills the stomach for a man; for a woman, there would be twenty-eight mouthfuls. (PiṇḍNi.

Wise men give to a companion in the holy life food that is one part less, half a part, or even a quarter of a part; likewise, they give what is equal to their own portion or even less. (Piṇḍa-Niyama 685)

In both villages and towns, one who consumes food and drink that are refined and excessively abundant, and does so too frequently— this should be understood as the fault of transgressing the proper measure. (Piṇḍaniryukti 686)
That which is more than thirty-two [mouthfuls], taken continuously and excessively,
and which moreover has its moisture drained— that the wise call "delicious" (*paṇīya*).
(Piṇḍaniyukti 687)
Having eaten food that is excessive in quantity, excessive in variety, or excessive in measure, one might suffer from vomiting, purging, or death; that is what is called indigestion. (PiṇḍNi 688)
One eats much, very much, or very frequently; or one eats three times, or more than that, or exactly that same excessive amount, or even when it is not yet time [to eat]. (Piṇḍaniryukti 689)
Those men who take food with shame, who take food with moderation, and who take little food—they do not treat themselves with medical science; they are the true physicians. (Piṇḍaniryukti 690)
A diet consisting of snake meat is superior to that of donkey, fish, and fermented gruel;
moreover, it removes disease and does not become a cause of disease. (Piṇḍaniryukti 691)
One should prepare half of the food with all its condiments;
for the liquid, one should make two parts, and for the purpose of allowing the movement of air, one should make it six parts less.
(PiṇḍNi 692)
Time is to be understood as threefold: cold, hot, and temperate.
Regarding the measure of food during that temperate time, it is as follows: PiṇḍNi.
Of cold liquid, one portion is for food, or four, or two for drinks; of hot liquid, however, there are two or three, while the remainder is for food. (Piṇḍaniyukti 694)
One part belongs to the master; two parts of the food remain, which may increase or decrease; for each [of these], there are two parts each. (Gāthā 696, Piṇḍaniryukti 695)
In that regard, the third and fourth parts are unstable, while the fifth, sixth, first, and second parts are stable. (PiṇḍNi.
That which one eats while being infatuated becomes "smoky"; furthermore, that which one eats while disparaging [others] becomes "with smoke. (Piṇḍaniyukti 697)

A burning piece of fuel that has become red-hot and is still emitting smoke is called "embers" (aṅgāra); however, when the smoke has ceased and it is merely burnt, it is [no longer so called]. (PiṇḍNi.
One who is consumed by the fire of passion, even while consuming pure food, quickly turns that fuel of conduct into something resembling burnt embers. (Piṇḍaniyukti 699)
As long as the fire of hatred burns, smoky with the smoke of lack of faith, and conduct remains like mere glowing embers, it will not consume [the fuel]. (Piṇḍaniyukti 700)

One should know that food accompanied by passion is like a fire with embers, and that accompanied by hatred is like a fire with smoke; thus, forty-six faults are to be understood regarding the rules for eating.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 701)
The ascetics consume food that is free from charcoal and free from smoke for the sake of meditation and study;
this is the instruction of the doctrine.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 702)
A monk practices the Dharma even while consuming food for six reasons,
and he practices it even while abstaining from food for exactly those same six reasons.
(Piṇḍaniyukti 703)

For the sake of alleviating pain, for the sake of service, for the sake of proper movement, for the sake of self-restraint, for the sake of sustaining life, and sixthly, for the sake of reflecting upon the Dharma. (Piṇḍaniryukti 704)
There is no pain equal to hunger; one should eat for the sake of pacifying it.
Since one who is hungry is unable to perform service (vaiyāvṛtya), therefore one should eat.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 705)

One who is not intent on recitation and reflection does not shine in the new [life], nor is he able to practice self-restraint; his conduct deteriorates, and he is unattached to the cultivation of virtues.
(Piṇḍaniryukti 706)

Alternatively, a self-restrained monk should not take food at all; rather, in the final part of the day, he should consume it only after considering six points, doing so sparingly and with moderation.
(Piṇḍaniyukti 707)

For the sake of enduring illness and hardships, for the protection of celibacy, for compassion toward living beings, and for the purpose of austerity through the emaciation of the body. (Piṇḍaniryukti 708)
Illness, old age, the proximity of kings and their officials, hardships for the sake of observing the vows of celibacy, compassion for living beings, rain, and excessive heat. (Piṇḍaniryukti 709)
For that reason, the austerity begins with the fourth meal and extends up to the sixth;
the sixth meal is for the purpose of bodily emaciation, and one remains without food. (Piṇḍaniryukti 710)
There are sixteen defects of procurement (*uggama-dosa*), sixteen defects of production (*uppāyaṇā-dosa*),
ten defects of seeking (*esaṇā-dosa*), and five [defects] beginning with mixing (*sañjōyaṇa*).
(Piṇḍaniyukti 711)

This is the rule for food as it has been taught by those who perceive all states of existence: one should act in such a way that the applications of the necessary duties of the Dharma do not decline. (Piṇḍaniryukti 712)

Whatever injury may occur to one who is striving, who is fully equipped with the scriptural rules, and who is endowed with internal purity, that results in the fruit of karmic exhaustion. (Piṇḍaniryukti 713)
